detailed_summary.v3.overview: This milestone Q&A was made after the channel crossed one million subscribers and focuses on the creator rather than fitness instruction. The speaker introduces himself, describes his education and earlier Infosys employment, and says his interest in fitness began during college. He explicitly says he was not a certified nutritionist at that time, though he had read extensively about modern nutrition and Ayurveda. He explains that FitTuber began because much online fitness content seemed focused on hardcore bodybuilding, leaving room for material aimed at ordinary people. His main advice to new creators is to prioritize content over expensive equipment; he says his first 50–60 videos were shot and edited on an iPhone 5s. He also says he was then doing the scripting, shooting and editing himself without a separate team. Other Q&A topics include the origin of the FitTuber name, earning more than at Infosys, using subscriber comments for encouragement when feeling low, his earlier theater experience, acting in videos for engagement and his personal choice to become vegetarian. The transcript also contains his opinion that Ayurveda is more accurate than modern nutrition science; that is retained as his viewpoint rather than presented as an established conclusion.

title_en.v1.title: FitTuber 2 Million Q&A: Sabbatical, Legal Battles, Patreon, Research Process, Indian Food and Future Plans
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript focuses on career changes, legal disputes, funding research, creator workflow, Indian food and future direction.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: This Q&A marks two million subscribers and centers on changes in the creator's work and channel strategy. He says he took a sabbatical from his job to focus on YouTube, moved to Delhi and was running two channels while remaining single. A major section discusses pushback from brands over his 'worst-to-best' videos: he reports video removals, legal notices and a difficult court experience, though these are self-reported claims within the transcript. He says he wants to deepen research beyond ingredient lists and use laboratory testing where useful, but such testing can be expensive. He therefore announces Patreon/FitTuber Club as a funding mechanism for research, lab work and legal costs while promising that regular channel content will remain free. The Q&A also includes a humorous section on improving spoken English through practice, a discussion of traditional Indian food and local produce, childhood photographs and a description of his research process. He says he prefers field research and expert conversations over relying only on online articles, while also giving strong weight to Ayurvedic texts for Ayurveda-focused content. He credits subscriber comments for motivation and says his future goals are health, spiritual growth and continuing to add value rather than pursuing large material ambitions.

title_en.v1.title: FitTuber 3 Million Q&A: Family, Nutrition Certifications, Ayurveda, Regional Channels and Sponsorship Choices
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript clearly covers family, training and certifications, Ayurveda, future regional-language channels and sponsorship selection.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The three-million-subscriber Q&A adds more detail about the creator's family, education and future channel plans. He introduces his mother, father and younger brother while saying his parents' faces are hidden because of threats and legal issues. He credits his father, who is involved in yoga, his mother, who helps with recipe content, and his younger brother, who assists with technology, for supporting the channel. He says memberships and Patreon enable more intensive research for ranking videos. A substantial section discusses education: the speaker says he completed a nutrition-related certification through NASM and was nearing completion of a fitness-coach certification from the International Sports Sciences Association, while describing his Ayurvedic learning as informal study of classical texts. He responds to criticism that the channel promotes pseudoscience by saying people should try Ayurveda and judge from experience; this is clearly his personal position. He then talks about plans to expand FitTuber into regional languages with native speakers. The final section explains that sponsorship choices are based primarily on ingredient lists rather than brand reputation, immediately followed by a sponsored hair-mask promotion whose safety claims are promotional rather than independently established. The video closes with a recurring marriage joke and thanks to the three-million-subscriber audience.
